abstract: Protein S-persulfidation, a post-translational modification mediated by hydrogen sulfide (H 2 S), plays an essential role in regulating protein function. However, current profiling methods, mainly based on liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS), tend to detect abundant proteins and often miss low-abundance but important regulators like transcription factors (TFs). To better understand the S-persulfidation landscape, we integrated datasets from three species— Homo sapiens , Mus musculus , and Arabidopsis thaliana —and found that TFs are strikingly underrepresented. To address this gap, we applied oxidative proteomics data from the Oximouse database, which reflects age-related redox changes, and identified hepatocyte nuclear factor 1α (HNF1α) as a candidate S-persulfidated TF. We confirmed that H 2 S induces S-persulfidation at Cys241 of HNF1α, disrupting its DNA binding through structural remodeling. This modification reduced PCSK9 expression, improved lipid profiles, and alleviated atherosclerosis in mice. Our study presents a cross-species strategy to uncover functional S-persulfidation targets and reveals a redox-based transcriptional mechanism involved in lipid metabolism and cardiovascular protection.

Materials

All animal experiments were performed in accordance with the International Guiding Principles for Biomedical Research Involving Animals. The study protocol was approved by Peking University First Hospital Animal Ethics Committee (Ethics No. J2022091).

2.3
Integration and analysis of Oximouse database
Oxidation proteomics data were obtained from the Oximouse database [
17
], which provides cysteine oxidation percentages in both young and aged mice across seven tissues: brain, heart, kidney, liver, lung, skeletal muscle (SKM), and spleen. To derive protein-level oxidation values, cysteine site-specific oxidation percentages were averaged arithmetically for each protein. The age-associated oxidation shift for each protein was quantified as: ΔOxidation% = Oxidation
Aged
% − Oxidation
Young
%. To calculate ΔOxidation%, NA values were excluded. Proteins with positive ΔOxidation% values were considered oxidation-prone during aging and were selected for downstream analysis. GO enrichment analysis of these age-oxidized proteins was performed using the
clusterProfiler
R package, retaining enriched terms with adjusted
p
-values <0.05. Functional classification of oxidation-prone proteins was conducted following the same annotation framework used in the analysis of the S-persulfidation dataset, allowing for consistent cross-comparison. Tissue-level redox connectivity networks were visualized using the
circlize
package (v0.4.16). Additional visualizations, including violin plots, bubble charts, and stacked bar plots, were generated using GraphPad Prism 8 and the R package
ggplot2
.
2.4
HepG2 cell culture
HepG2 cells (RRID: CVCL_0027) were purchased from the Cell Bank of Chinese Academy of Sciences in December 2015. The cell line has been tested and confirmed to be free of mycoplasma contamination. HepG2 cells were cultured in MEM supplemented with 10 % FBS at 37 °C under 5 % CO
2
in a humidified incubator. When cells reached 80–90 % confluence, they were synchronized by culturing in serum-free MEM for 24 h, then incubated with or without NaHS (100 μM) for 48 h.
2.5
Recombinant protein of human HNF1α
Recombinant human wild type (WT) HNF1α and its C241S mutant were purchased from Origene (Rockville, MD, USA; catalog number TP311201). Proteins were expressed in HEK293T cells and purified to >80 % purity, as verified by SDS-PAGE and Coomassie staining.
2.6
Plasmid transfection
Human WT HNF1α and C241S mutant plasmids in the pENTER vector were purchased from Vigene Biosciences (Shandong, China). HepG2 cells were transfected with WT or mutant HNF1α plasmids using jetPEI reagent according to the manufacturer's instructions. Cells were harvested 48 h post-transfection for subsequent analyses.
2.7
HNF1α S-persulfidation detected by “Tag-Switch” analysis
HNF1α S-persulfidation was detected using the “Tag-Switch” method based on selective biotin labeling of S-persulfidated cysteines, rather than antibody-based recognition [
43
,
44
]. Briefly, HepG2 cells or frozen mouse liver tissues were lysed by ultrasonication in HEN buffer (250 mM HEPES, 50 mM NaCl, 1 mM EDTA, 0.1 mM neocuproine, 1 % NP-40) supplemented with protease inhibitors. Lysates were incubated with 50 mM methylsulfonyl benzothiazole (MSBT-A), a sulfhydryl-reactive blocking reagent, at 37 °C for 1 h to block free thiols. After desalting, persulfidated cysteines were selectively tagged by incubating samples with 20 mM biotin-linked cyanoacetate (
C
N-biotin) containing 2.5 % SDS at 37 °C for 1 h. Excess
C
N-biotin was removed by desalting, and biotin-tagged proteins were captured using high-capacity streptavidin agarose beads (Thermo Fisher Scientific) overnight at 4 °C. After extensive washing, proteins were eluted with 4 × non-reducing Laemmli buffer (Bio-Rad), boiled at 95 °C for 10 min, and analyzed by Western blot using
anti
-HNF1α antibody. To ensure reproducibility, all Tag-Switch experiments were independently repeated three times using both HepG2 cells and mouse liver tissues, yielding consistent detection of the biotin-labeled HNF1α signal.
2.8
HNF1α S-persulfidation detected by LC-MS/MS
Purified recombinant human HNF1α protein was divided into three groups: control, NaHS-treated, and NaHS plus dithiothreitol (DTT)-treated. The NaHS group was incubated with 100 μM NaHS at 37 °C for 1 h; the NaHS + DTT group was incubated with NaHS for 1 h followed by 10 mM DTT for 30 min; the control group was treated with the same volume of PBS. All samples were alkylated with 20 mM iodoacetamide (IAA) at 25 °C for 30 min in the dark, separated by SDS-PAGE, stained with Coomassie blue, and subjected to overnight tryptic digestion at 37 °C. Peptides were dried, reconstituted, and analyzed by LC-MS/MS on an Ultimate 3000 LC system coupled to a Q-Exactive Plus Orbitrap mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher) as previously reported [
45
]. For identification of cysteine modifications, raw mass spectrometry data were searched using pFind 3.0 (
http://pfind.ict.ac.cn/software/pFind3/index.html
) with an expanded variable modification list that included persulfidation and polysulfidation (–SSH, –SSSH, –SSSSH, –SSSSSH), sulfenylation and higher oxidation states (–SOH, –SO
2
H, –SO
3
H), S-nitrosylation (–SNO), and S-glutathiolation (–SSG). The thermo. raw files can be obtained from the ProteomeXchange Consortium (
http://proteomecentral.proteomexchange.org
) via the iProX [
46
] (accession no. PXD068170).
2.9
Electrophoretic mobility shift assay (EMSA) for the detection of DNA binding activity of HNF1α
Nuclear extracts were prepared using a commercial kit (Thermo Fisher, USA) [
47
]. DIG-ddUTP-labeled double-stranded oligonucleotide probes (PCSK9-HNF1α-forward: 5′-agtccgggggttccgttaatgtttaatcagataggatc-3’; PCSK9-HNF1α-reverse: 5′-gatcctatctgattaaacattaacggaacccccggact-3′) were incubated with nuclear protein at room temperature, followed by electrophoresis and electroblotting.
2.10
HNF1α-DNA interaction quantitated by surface plasmon resonance (SPR)
DNA binding affinities of WT and C241S HNF1α proteins were analyzed on a Biacore T200 system (GE Healthcare, Chicago, IL, USA) at 25 °C using running buffer (pH 7.4). Biotinylated DNA probes (sequence as in EMSA) were immobilized on a streptavidin sensor chip (∼400 RU). Proteins, pretreated with or without 100 μM NaHS at 37 °C for 1 h, were injected at various concentrations for 60 s association and 100 s dissociation. Sensor surface was regenerated with 1.25 M NaCl after each run. Data were fitted with BIA evaluation 2.0 software to calculate kinetic parameters.
2.11
Homology modeling method and MD simulation
The HNF1α protein/DNA complex structure was constructed using homology modeling. The amber14sb_parmbsc1 force field (ff14SB for protein and parmbsc1 for DNA) was applied in MD simulations [
48
,
49
]. The S-persulfidated cysteine was parameterized using the General AMBER Force Field (GAFF), with atomic charges derived via Multiwfn v3.6 (dev) [
49
]. The complex was solvated in a TIP3P water box (∼8.37 × 8.98 × 7.42 nm
3
), neutralized with Na
+
, and physiological ionic strength (0.15 M NaCl) was maintained. MD simulations were performed with GROMACS 2018.3 [
50
], including energy minimization (steepest descent), 1 ns NVT and 1 ns NPT equilibrations, followed by three independent 100-ns production runs in the NPT ensemble. Subsequently, three independent 100-ns production run was conducted in the NPT ensemble for both systems. Visualizations were generated using VMD v1.9.3 [
51
].
2.12
CSE knockout (CSE KO) mice
CSE
heterozygous mice on a C57BL/6J background were kindly provided by Prof. Bin Geng (Fuwai Hospital, Beijing, China). The second exon of the
CSE
gene was replaced with a neomycin cassette by homologous recombination to generate knockout mice. Male CSE KO and WT littermates (12 weeks old, n = 6 per group) were bred in-house under standard laboratory conditions (22 ± 2 °C, 12 h light/dark cycle, ad libitum food and water). Genotyping was performed by PCR of tail DNA using primers: 5′-CCTGGATATAAGCGCCAAAG-3′, 5′-AGGAACCAGGGCGTATCTCT-3′, and 5′-CGAGAATTCCATTGCTCAGG-3'. CSE mRNA and protein expression in liver tissues were confirmed by RT-qPCR and Western blotting, respectively.
2.13
Detection of H
2
S content in situ using a fluorescent H
2
S probe
The H
2
S fluorescent probe Mito-HS [
52
] was kindly provided by Prof. Xinjing Tang (Peking University Health Science Center, Beijing, China). Frozen liver sections were rehydrated in PBS and incubated with the fluorescent H
2
S probe Mito-HS (100 μM) in the dark for 30 min, followed by PBS washes. Nuclei were counterstained with DAPI mounting medium (ZSGB-Bio, Beijing, China). Fluorescence imaging was performed using confocal laser scanning microscopy to visualize H
2
S (green) and nuclei (blue) signals.
2.14
RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq)
Total RNA was extracted from liver tissues of 12-week-old male CSE KO and WT mice using TRIzol reagent. The method of RNA-seq was described previously [
53
]. Briefly, RNA quality was assessed with Qubit 2.0 and Bioanalyzer 2100; only samples with RIN >8 were used. Libraries were prepared with the NEBNext® Ultra™ RNA Library Prep Kit and sequenced on Illumina HiSeq 4000 (150 bp paired-end reads) by Novogene Co., Ltd. After adapter trimming and quality filtering, reads were aligned to the mouse genome (Ensembl release 81) using TopHat v2.0.9, achieving >92 % mapping rate. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were defined using Cufflinks v2.1.1 with q < 0.05 and fold change >1.5. GO enrichment was performed to identify significant biological processes (
p
< 0.05).
2.15
Chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) analysis for the detection of DNA binding level of HNF1α with PCSK9 promoter
ChIP was performed using the EpiQuik™ kit (Epigentek, Farmingdale, NY, USA) per the manufacturer's instructions. HepG2 cells were fixed with 1 % paraformaldehyde, lysed, and chromatin was sheared by sonication to 200–1000 bp fragments. Immunoprecipitation was conducted with 10 μL HNF1α antibody. After reversal of crosslinking and DNA purification, PCR amplification of the PCSK9 promoter region was performed using primers: forward 5′-TCCAGCCCAGTTAGGATTTG-3′, reverse 5′-CACACCCTAGAAGGTTTCCG-3’.
2.16
Luciferase reporter assay detection of PCSK9 promotor activity
The PCSK9 promoter luciferase reporter constructs were generated as previously described [
54
,
55
]. Briefly, the human PCSK9 promoter was PCR-amplified from human genomic DNA and cloned into the pGL3-Basic vector. Primer sequences were as follows: forward 5′-ATCGACTCGAGGGAGGATATGGGATGAGAAGTG-3′ and reverse 5′-AGCTGAAGCTTACTGTGCAGGAGCTGAAGTTC-3’. The HNF1α mutant construct (HNF1α-Mut) was generated using site-directed mutagenesis with sense oligonucleotide 5′-agtccgggggttccTGGaatgtttaatcagataggatc-3′ following the manufacturer's protocol [
56
]. HepG2 cells were transfected with WT or mutant PCSK9 promoter reporter plasmids together with Renilla luciferase plasmid as a transfection control at a ratio of 20:1 using jetPEI reagent. After 24 h, the medium was replaced with basal MEM and incubated overnight. Cells were then lipid-loaded and treated with or without 100 μM NaHS for 48 h, after which luciferase activities were measured.
2.17
Detection of the protein degradation rate
Lipid-loaded HepG2 cells were treated with 100 μM NaHS and subsequently incubated with 50 μg/mL Chx for indicated times. Control cells (t = 0) received an equivalent volume of DMSO. Cells were lysed and analyzed by Western blot as described. Band intensity of PCSK9 was normalized to β-actin, then to the t = 0 control, and expressed as percentages. Protein degradation kinetics were fitted to a linear regression: y = ax + b, where y = log
10
(relative protein level), x = Chx incubation time. Protein half-life was calculated when y corresponded to log
10
50 % of initial protein level.
2.18
Mouse model of atherosclerosis and grouping
Male
Apoe
−/−
mice (6 weeks old, n = 36) were obtained from Beijing HFK Bioscience Co., Ltd (China) and randomly assigned into two groups (n = 18 per group) receiving adeno-associated virus serotype 8 (AAV8) vectors expressing either Flag-tagged WT HNF1α or C241S mutant HNF1α under the liver-specific TBG promoter (AAV8-TBG-Flag-WT or AAV8-TBG-Flag-C241S) [
57
]. Each mouse received 5 × 10
11
genome copies of virus in 100 μL via tail vein injection. Two weeks post-injection, mice in each group were further subdivided into control and NaHS treatment groups (n = 9 per subgroup). NaHS groups were fed a HCD (40 % kcal fat, 1.25 % cholesterol, 0.5 % sodium cholate; SYSE Bio, D12109C) [
[58]
,
[59]
,
[60]
,
[61]
] and received daily i. p. injections of NaHS (56 μmol/kg) for 10 weeks. Control groups were fed the same diet and injected with the same volume of saline. After a 6-h fast, venous blood was collected. Mice were euthanized by cervical dislocation. Liver tissues were snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C. Hearts and aortas were fixed in 4 % paraformaldehyde at 4 °C for at least 24 h. After removing perivascular tissues, aortas were opened longitudinally, fixed on black wax discs, stained with Oil Red O for 30 min, rinsed with 60 % isopropanol, and imaged. Hearts were cryoprotected in 20 % sucrose, embedded in OCT compound, and serial 7-μm aortic root sections were prepared for Oil Red O staining. Lesion areas were quantified using Image-Pro Plus 6.0 software. All animal procedures were approved by the Peking University First Hospital Animal Ethics Committee (J2022091).
2.19
Detection of H
2
S content using a polarographic H
2
S sensor
H
2
S levels in plasma was measured using a polarographic H
2
S sensor system (ISO–H
2
S-100 sensor coupled with Free Radical Analyzer TBR4100, WPI, Sarasota, FL, USA) as previously described [
62
]. The sensor was polarized in PBS for 2 h until stable current was achieved, then calibrated with Na
2
S standards (0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, and 16 μM). Samples were measured at 10 mm immersion depth, and H
2
S concentrations were calculated from the calibration curve.
2.20
Measurement of plasma lipids
The plasma was separated by centrifugation at 3000 rpm for 15 min at 4 °C and stored at −80 °C. The levels of total cholesterol, LDL-C, and triglyceride in plasma were analyzed using the surface-active agent cleaning method (Hitachi 7600-110, Tokyo).
2.21
Western blot analysis
Frozen mouse liver tissues or cultured cells were lysed in ice-cold lysis buffer to extract proteins. Protein concentration was measured by the Bradford assay. Equal amounts of protein (60 μg) were separated by SDS-PAGE and transferred to membranes by electroblotting. Membranes were blocked and incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies, followed by incubation with horseradish peroxidase-conjugated secondary antibodies (Sigma, USA). Protein bands were visualized using chemiluminescence. Primary antibodies used included: HNF1α (1:1000, CST 89670S), β-Actin (1:5000, ZSGB-Bio TA-09), GAPDH (1:5000, ZSGB-Bio TA-08), PCSK9 (1:1000, Abcam ab52754), and CSE (1:1000, Proteintech 12217-1-AP).
2.22
RT-qPCR measurement
Total RNA was extracted from mouse liver tissues or HepG2 cells and reverse-transcribed to cDNA. PCR amplification was performed under the following conditions: 95 °C for 5 min; 40 cycles of 95 °C for 15 s and 60 °C for 1 min. Primer sequences are listed below (forward, reverse):
CSE
(mouse) (5′-GCAATGGAATTCTCGTGCCG-3′, 5′-GCAGCCACTGCTTTTTCCAA-3′),
Pcsk9
(mouse) (5′-ATCACCGACTTCAACAGCGT-3′, 5′-GCCCTTCCCTTGACAGTTGA-3′),
PCSK9
(human) (5′-CGAGGAGGACGGGACCCGC-3′, 5′-ATGGTCACCGACTTCGAGAATG-3′),
Abcc3
(mouse) (5′-ACTCTCATGTGGCGAAGCAT-3′, 5′-GATAAAGTCCGTCTGGGGCA-3′),
Mvd
(mouse) (5′-CCACAACCGTTGCCATTAGC-3′, 5′-GTAGAGTGTCCCCGTCCTCT-3′),
Hmgcs1
(mouse) (5′-CTGATCCCCTTTGGCTCTTTCA-3′, 5′-CCCAGGCCGATGGTATACTT-3′),
Gapdh
(mouse) (5′-TGTGTCCGTCGTGGATCTGA-3′, 5′-ATGCCTGCTTCACCACCTTCT-3′),
GAPDH
(human) (5′-CGTCGCCAGCCGAGCCACA-3′, 5′- CAGTCAGCCGCATCTTCTTTT-3′).
Relative gene expression was calculated using the 2-
Δ(ΔCT)
method.
2.23
Statistical analysis
Data are presented as mean ± SEM. Statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism 8 and SPSS 16.0 (SPSS Inc., Chicago, IL, USA). Normality was assessed by Shapiro-Wilk test. Variance equality was evaluated using F-test for two groups and Bartlett's test for multiple groups. For normally distributed data, two-group comparisons were analyzed by Student's t-test (equal variance) or Welch's
t
-test (unequal variance). Multiple-group comparisons were performed by one-way ANOVA followed by Bonferroni's post hoc test (equal variance) or Welch's ANOVA with Games-Howell post hoc test (unequal variance). For non-normally distributed data or small sample sizes (n < 6), nonparametric tests were applied: Mann-Whitney
U
test for two-group comparisons and Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn's post hoc for multiple groups. Exact
p
values were shown in figures, and
p
< 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Biological replicates are denoted by n.

Introduction
Protein S-persulfidation, a reversible post-translational modification (PTM) of cysteine residues mediated by hydrogen sulfide (H
2
S), has emerged as a critical regulator of cellular redox homeostasis and metabolic adaptation. Increasing evidence suggests that S-persulfidation plays a protective role against oxidative stress by preventing irreversible cysteine overoxidation, thereby conferring preventive/therapeutic effects in a variety of diseases, such as cardiovascular, immune, and neurodegenerative disorders [
[1]
,
[2]
,
[3]
].
With the development of chemical labeling and LC-MS/MS-based techniques, large-scale profiling of S-persulfidome has been achieved across multiple species and tissues [
2
,
4
,
5
]. These studies have led to the identification of hundreds of S-persulfidation targets, and functional investigations have primarily focused on two categories of proteins: enzymes and transcription factors (TFs). Enzymes are often selected due to their well-characterized catalytic cysteines and measurable activity changes [
6
,
7
]. For instance, glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH) was the first identified target with cysteine (Cys) 152 S-persulfidation enhancing its enzymatic activity and promoting glycolysis [
8
]. TFs have attracted considerable attention because they are central regulators of gene expression and cellular responses [
9
]. By binding to specific promoter elements, TFs activate or repress transcription, thereby orchestrating adaptive responses to environmental and metabolic cues [
10
,
11
]. For example, H
2
S-mediated S-persulfidation of the p65 subunit of nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB) at Cys38 reduces DNA binding and alleviates inflammation [
12
]. However, most studies identifying TFs as S-persulfidated substrates have relied on targeted biochemical approaches, rather than direct hits from proteomic screens [
13
]. Furthermore, there remains a lack of detailed characterization regarding how the S-persulfidation structurally and functionally regulates transcriptional activity.
To overcome these limitations, we designed a multi-layered proteomic strategy. Mechanistically, S-persulfidation can occur via two non-exclusive pathways: first, cysteine thiols are partially oxidized (e.g., to sulfenic acids or disulfides) and subsequently react with HS
−
; second, HS
−
may be converted under physiological conditions into reactive sulfur species, which can directly drive persulfidation. Both mechanisms converge on the chemical principle that S-persulfidation protects cysteines from irreversible overoxidation [
2
,
[14]
,
[15]
,
[16]
]. Leveraging this understanding, we integrated published S-persulfidation datasets across species, revealing a striking underrepresentation of TFs despite their functional importance. Then, based on the chemical premise that S-persulfidation prevents cysteine overoxidation, we used the Oximouse redox proteomic atlas [
17
] to identify candidate TF targets undetected by conventional S-persulfidomics, ultimately highlighting hepatocyte nuclear factor 1α (HNF1α) as a previously unrecognized S-persulfidation target and providing a basis for exploring its regulatory role.
HNF1α is a liver-enriched TF that expressed in organs such as the liver, kidney, pancreas, and intestine [
18
]. Structurally, HNF1α comprises an
N
-terminal dimerization domain (DD), a central DNA-binding domain (DBD), and a
C
-terminal transactivation domain (TAD) [
19
]. Among these, the DBD is essential for recognizing and binding to specific DNA sequences, thereby determining the transcriptional specificity of HNF1α [
20
]. The DBD consists of a Pit-OctUnc-specific (POU
S
) domain and a homeodomain (POU
H
), which are connected by a flexible loop that allows structural adaptability during DNA interaction [
21
]. Notably, HNF1α contains three cysteine residues (Cys50, Cys236, and Cys241), among which Cys241 locates in the POU
H
domain [
22
]. Functionally, a mutation of Cys241 to glycine has been identified in maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY) patients but not in healthy individuals [
23
]. Moreover, HNF1α-MODY patients seem to be more prone to an early atherosclerotic phenotype [
24
], suggesting a role for Cys241 in glycolipid metabolic homeostasis. As aging increases HNF1α oxidation in the liver (Oximouse dataset), and the known role of S-persulfidation in protecting cysteines from overoxidation, we hypothesized that S-persulfidation might similarly preserve HNF1α function under redox stress. However, whether HNF1α is S-persulfidated and how this affects its transcriptional activity remain unknown.
In this study, we identified Cys241 of HNF1α as a novel S-persulfidation site targeted by H
2
S. This modification impaired its DNA-binding capacity and transcriptional activity, as demonstrated by molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and structural analyses. Transcriptomic profiling of livers from cystathionine γ-lyase (CSE, also known as CTH) knockout mice further revealed proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9) as a downstream target suppressed by S-persulfidated HNF1α. PCSK9 as a target gene of HNF1α promotes low-density lipoprotein receptor (LDLR) degradation and then results in increased plasma low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), thereby contributing to dyslipidemia and cardiovascular disease [
25
,
26
]. The repression of PCSK9 expression by HNF1α S-persulfidation highlights the role of HNF1α in lipid metabolic regulation. Finally, using a high-cholesterol diet (HCD)-induced atherosclerosis model, we demonstrated that HNF1α S-persulfidation alleviated lipid accumulation and vascular pathology, underscoring its protective function in redox-regulated metabolic disorders. This work not only reveals that S-persulfidation functions as a regulatory switch for TFs involved in metabolic control, but also offers a blueprint for identifying functional S-persulfidation targets beyond the limits of current detection technologies.

2.3
Integration and analysis of Oximouse database
Oxidation proteomics data were obtained from the Oximouse database [
17
], which provides cysteine oxidation percentages in both young and aged mice across seven tissues: brain, heart, kidney, liver, lung, skeletal muscle (SKM), and spleen. To derive protein-level oxidation values, cysteine site-specific oxidation percentages were averaged arithmetically for each protein. The age-associated oxidation shift for each protein was quantified as: ΔOxidation% = Oxidation
Aged
% − Oxidation
Young
%. To calculate ΔOxidation%, NA values were excluded. Proteins with positive ΔOxidation% values were considered oxidation-prone during aging and were selected for downstream analysis. GO enrichment analysis of these age-oxidized proteins was performed using the
clusterProfiler
R package, retaining enriched terms with adjusted
p
-values <0.05. Functional classification of oxidation-prone proteins was conducted following the same annotation framework used in the analysis of the S-persulfidation dataset, allowing for consistent cross-comparison. Tissue-level redox connectivity networks were visualized using the
circlize
package (v0.4.16). Additional visualizations, including violin plots, bubble charts, and stacked bar plots, were generated using GraphPad Prism 8 and the R package
ggplot2
.
2.4
HepG2 cell culture
HepG2 cells (RRID: CVCL_0027) were purchased from the Cell Bank of Chinese Academy of Sciences in December 2015. The cell line has been tested and confirmed to be free of mycoplasma contamination. HepG2 cells were cultured in MEM supplemented with 10 % FBS at 37 °C under 5 % CO
2
in a humidified incubator. When cells reached 80–90 % confluence, they were synchronized by culturing in serum-free MEM for 24 h, then incubated with or without NaHS (100 μM) for 48 h.
2.5
Recombinant protein of human HNF1α
Recombinant human wild type (WT) HNF1α and its C241S mutant were purchased from Origene (Rockville, MD, USA; catalog number TP311201). Proteins were expressed in HEK293T cells and purified to >80 % purity, as verified by SDS-PAGE and Coomassie staining.
2.6
Plasmid transfection
Human WT HNF1α and C241S mutant plasmids in the pENTER vector were purchased from Vigene Biosciences (Shandong, China). HepG2 cells were transfected with WT or mutant HNF1α plasmids using jetPEI reagent according to the manufacturer's instructions. Cells were harvested 48 h post-transfection for subsequent analyses.
2.7
HNF1α S-persulfidation detected by “Tag-Switch” analysis
HNF1α S-persulfidation was detected using the “Tag-Switch” method based on selective biotin labeling of S-persulfidated cysteines, rather than antibody-based recognition [
43
,
44
]. Briefly, HepG2 cells or frozen mouse liver tissues were lysed by ultrasonication in HEN buffer (250 mM HEPES, 50 mM NaCl, 1 mM EDTA, 0.1 mM neocuproine, 1 % NP-40) supplemented with protease inhibitors. Lysates were incubated with 50 mM methylsulfonyl benzothiazole (MSBT-A), a sulfhydryl-reactive blocking reagent, at 37 °C for 1 h to block free thiols. After desalting, persulfidated cysteines were selectively tagged by incubating samples with 20 mM biotin-linked cyanoacetate (
C
N-biotin) containing 2.5 % SDS at 37 °C for 1 h. Excess
C
N-biotin was removed by desalting, and biotin-tagged proteins were captured using high-capacity streptavidin agarose beads (Thermo Fisher Scientific) overnight at 4 °C. After extensive washing, proteins were eluted with 4 × non-reducing Laemmli buffer (Bio-Rad), boiled at 95 °C for 10 min, and analyzed by Western blot using
anti
-HNF1α antibody. To ensure reproducibility, all Tag-Switch experiments were independently repeated three times using both HepG2 cells and mouse liver tissues, yielding consistent detection of the biotin-labeled HNF1α signal.
2.8
HNF1α S-persulfidation detected by LC-MS/MS
Purified recombinant human HNF1α protein was divided into three groups: control, NaHS-treated, and NaHS plus dithiothreitol (DTT)-treated. The NaHS group was incubated with 100 μM NaHS at 37 °C for 1 h; the NaHS + DTT group was incubated with NaHS for 1 h followed by 10 mM DTT for 30 min; the control group was treated with the same volume of PBS. All samples were alkylated with 20 mM iodoacetamide (IAA) at 25 °C for 30 min in the dark, separated by SDS-PAGE, stained with Coomassie blue, and subjected to overnight tryptic digestion at 37 °C. Peptides were dried, reconstituted, and analyzed by LC-MS/MS on an Ultimate 3000 LC system coupled to a Q-Exactive Plus Orbitrap mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher) as previously reported [
45
]. For identification of cysteine modifications, raw mass spectrometry data were searched using pFind 3.0 (
http://pfind.ict.ac.cn/software/pFind3/index.html
) with an expanded variable modification list that included persulfidation and polysulfidation (–SSH, –SSSH, –SSSSH, –SSSSSH), sulfenylation and higher oxidation states (–SOH, –SO
2
H, –SO
3
H), S-nitrosylation (–SNO), and S-glutathiolation (–SSG). The thermo. raw files can be obtained from the ProteomeXchange Consortium (
http://proteomecentral.proteomexchange.org
) via the iProX [
46
] (accession no. PXD068170).
2.9
Electrophoretic mobility shift assay (EMSA) for the detection of DNA binding activity of HNF1α
Nuclear extracts were prepared using a commercial kit (Thermo Fisher, USA) [
47
]. DIG-ddUTP-labeled double-stranded oligonucleotide probes (PCSK9-HNF1α-forward: 5′-agtccgggggttccgttaatgtttaatcagataggatc-3’; PCSK9-HNF1α-reverse: 5′-gatcctatctgattaaacattaacggaacccccggact-3′) were incubated with nuclear protein at room temperature, followed by electrophoresis and electroblotting.
2.10
HNF1α-DNA interaction quantitated by surface plasmon resonance (SPR)
DNA binding affinities of WT and C241S HNF1α proteins were analyzed on a Biacore T200 system (GE Healthcare, Chicago, IL, USA) at 25 °C using running buffer (pH 7.4). Biotinylated DNA probes (sequence as in EMSA) were immobilized on a streptavidin sensor chip (∼400 RU). Proteins, pretreated with or without 100 μM NaHS at 37 °C for 1 h, were injected at various concentrations for 60 s association and 100 s dissociation. Sensor surface was regenerated with 1.25 M NaCl after each run. Data were fitted with BIA evaluation 2.0 software to calculate kinetic parameters.
2.11
Homology modeling method and MD simulation
The HNF1α protein/DNA complex structure was constructed using homology modeling. The amber14sb_parmbsc1 force field (ff14SB for protein and parmbsc1 for DNA) was applied in MD simulations [
48
,
49
]. The S-persulfidated cysteine was parameterized using the General AMBER Force Field (GAFF), with atomic charges derived via Multiwfn v3.6 (dev) [
49
]. The complex was solvated in a TIP3P water box (∼8.37 × 8.98 × 7.42 nm
3
), neutralized with Na
+
, and physiological ionic strength (0.15 M NaCl) was maintained. MD simulations were performed with GROMACS 2018.3 [
50
], including energy minimization (steepest descent), 1 ns NVT and 1 ns NPT equilibrations, followed by three independent 100-ns production runs in the NPT ensemble. Subsequently, three independent 100-ns production run was conducted in the NPT ensemble for both systems. Visualizations were generated using VMD v1.9.3 [
51
].

CSE

Male CSE KO and WT littermates (12 weeks old, n = 6 per group) were bred in-house under standard laboratory conditions (22 ± 2 °C, 12 h light/dark cycle, ad libitum food and water). RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq)
Total RNA was extracted from liver tissues of 12-week-old male CSE KO and WT mice using TRIzol reagent. The method of RNA-seq was described previously [
53

Chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) analysis for the detection of DNA binding level of HNF1α with PCSK9 promoter
ChIP was performed using the EpiQuik™ kit (Epigentek, Farmingdale, NY, USA) per the manufacturer's instructions. HepG2 cells were fixed with 1 % paraformaldehyde, lysed, and chromatin was sheared by sonication to 200–1000 bp fragments. Immunoprecipitation was conducted with 10 μL HNF1α antibody. After reversal of crosslinking and DNA purification, PCR amplification of the PCSK9 promoter region was performed using primers: forward 5′-TCCAGCCCAGTTAGGATTTG-3′, reverse 5′-CACACCCTAGAAGGTTTCCG-3’.

The PCSK9 promoter luciferase reporter constructs were generated as previously described [

Primer sequences were as follows: forward 5′-ATCGACTCGAGGGAGGATATGGGATGAGAAGTG-3′ and reverse 5′-AGCTGAAGCTTACTGTGCAGGAGCTGAAGTTC-3’. The HNF1α mutant construct (HNF1α-Mut) was generated using site-directed mutagenesis with sense oligonucleotide 5′-agtccgggggttccTGGaatgtttaatcagataggatc-3′ following the manufacturer's protocol [

After 24 h, the medium was replaced with basal MEM and incubated overnight. Cells were then lipid-loaded and treated with or without 100 μM NaHS for 48 h, after which luciferase activities were measured.

Detection of the protein degradation rate
Lipid-loaded HepG2 cells were treated with 100 μM NaHS and subsequently incubated with 50 μg/mL Chx for indicated times. Control cells (t = 0) received an equivalent volume of DMSO. Cells were lysed and analyzed by Western blot as described. Band intensity of PCSK9 was normalized to β-actin, then to the t = 0 control, and expressed as percentages. Mouse model of atherosclerosis and grouping
Male
Apoe
−/−

[60]

[61]

3.1
The scarcity of TFs in the S-persulfidome datasets contrasts with their prominence in biological research
To gain a comprehensive understanding of the biological significance of protein S-persulfidation, we first collected and curated fourteen high-confidence S-persulfidome datasets from three species:
Homo sapiens
,
Mus musculus
, and
Arabidopsis thaliana
(
Table 1
;
Table S1
). To ensure that the combined dataset was not disproportionately biased by a few studies, we quantified the relative contribution of each dataset to the final union (
Fig. S1
). GO enrichment analysis was performed separately using the
clusterProfiler
package, and a total of 42 GO biological process terms with significant enrichment (
p
< 0.05) were found to overlap across all three species (
Table S2
). To gain a holistic view of the enriched functions, we visualized the 42 terms using a word cloud. Notably, terms related to “metabolism' were highly prominent, suggesting a conserved role of S-persulfidation in metabolic regulation across species (
Fig. 1
A). To further verify this functional pattern using an orthogonal approach, we conducted KEGG pathway enrichment analysis via DAVID (
Table S2
). Again, we intersected significant pathways (
p
< 0.05) among the three species and identified 26 common entries, the majority of which were related to metabolic pathways such as glycolysis/gluconeogenesis, fatty acid degradation, and purine metabolism (
Fig. 1
B). These results collectively reinforce the idea that S-persulfidation represents an evolutionarily conserved post-translational modification associated with the regulation of metabolism.
Next, we classified the S-persulfidated proteins functionally into enzymes, transcription regulators, translation regulators, transporters/channels, chaperones/folding proteins, and structural/scaffolding/binding proteins (
Table S3
). Despite differences in biological systems and detection platforms, a common pattern emerged: enzymes represented the most abundant protein category across all three species, accounting for 36 % in
Homo sapiens
, 46 % in
Mus musculus
, and 27 % in
Arabidopsis thaliana
, which underscores their pivotal roles in fundamental cellular processes (
Fig. 1
C). In contrast, proteins annotated as TFs were sparsely represented: only 4 %, 2 %, and 1 % in
Homo sapiens
,
Mus musculus
, and
Arabid
opsis thaliana datasets, respectively (
Fig. 1
C).
This trend contrasts with the functional importance of TFs observed in published studies. We curated 58 S-persulfidated proteins from recent review articles with validated experimental evidence (
Table S3
) [
13
,
[63]
,
[64]
,
[65]
]. Among these, enzymes accounted for the largest group (n = 29, 50 %), but strikingly, TFs constituted the second most frequent category (n = 17, ∼29 %)—far exceeding their proportion in the proteomic datasets (
Fig. 1
D). This list includes well-known redox-sensitive transcriptional regulators such as the p65 subunit of NF-κB [
66
], signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3) [
67
], and abscisic acid-insensitive 4 (ABI4)—a positive regulator in ABA signaling, which is essential for seed germination and seedling growth [
68
,
69
]. These data point to a critical gap: despite being underrepresented in large-scale proteomic datasets, TFs appear to be key functional targets of S-persulfidation.
To explore the origin of this discrepancy, we turned to protein abundance profiles across species using PaxDb (
Table S4
). We observed that TFs are generally distributed in the low-abundance range, whereas enzymes and structural proteins are primarily of medium to high abundance (
Fig. 1
E). Since current mass spectrometry techniques—especially those relying on data-dependent acquisition (DDA)—are biased toward more abundant proteins [
70
,
71
], TFs may frequently fall below the detection threshold. Thus, proteomic approaches alone are insufficient to capture the full repertoire of functionally important S-persulfidation targets.
Given this challenge, we sought alternative strategies to identify such candidates. From a chemical perspective, S-persulfidation is believed to occur on cysteines that are initially oxidized to sulfenic acid (–SOH) (
Fig. 1
F). Without further protection, these intermediates can be irreversibly oxidized to sulfinic (–SO
2
H) or sulfonic acid (–SO
3
H), leading to protein dysfunction (
Fig. 1
F). S-persulfidation, in this context, serves as a protective modification. This rationale prompted us to explore oxidation proteomics data to identify candidate S-persulfidated proteins missed by direct S-persulfidation profiling.

Oxidative proteomic database Oximouse provides novel insights for uncovering potential functional S-persulfidated TFs
Building on the premise that oxidized proteins might serve as reservoirs for S-persulfidation modifications, we utilized Oximouse, a comprehensive age-resolved oxidative proteomics dataset across mouse organs, including brain, heart, kidney, liver, lung, SKM, and spleen. As an initial step, we re-analyzed this dataset to identify proteins exhibiting age-dependent oxidation (
Fig. 2
A;
Table S5
). Interestingly, within each organ, a subset of proteins displayed reduced oxidation with aging, indicating that aging involves not only increases but also decreases in oxidative modifications. These observations highlight the importance of protein-level analyses to pinpoint age-sensitive proteins that may act as potential persulfidation targets. Given that oxidative stress is a hallmark of aging and S-persulfidation confers protective effects in age-related diseases [
72
,
73
], we focused on proteins with age-associated increases in oxidation as candidate S-persulfidation targets, aiming to uncover their potential roles in mitigating oxidative damage via organ-specific biological processes.

In light of the robust association between S-persulfidation and metabolism revealed earlier, we specifically examined the liver, a central metabolic organ. Using the site-level cysteine oxidation data of seven tissues from Oximouse, we constructed a chord diagram to visualize inter-organ redox connectivity (

S-persulfidation. In WT HNF1α-expressing mice, NaHS treatment significantly reduced hepatic PCSK9 mRNA and protein levels (
Fig. 6
D and E), increased hepatic LDLR protein expression (
Fig. 6
E), lowered plasma total cholesterol and LDL-C levels (
Fig. S8
), but had no effect on plasma triglyceride content (
Fig. S8
). Accordingly, atherosclerotic burden was markedly alleviated in the NaHS-treated WT group, as evidenced by reduced plaque formation along the entire aorta and in the aortic root (
Fig. 6
F and G). In contrast, NaHS treatment failed to reduce PCSK9 expression or atherosclerotic plaque area in mice expressing C241S HNF1α, whose S-persulfidation was abolished (
Fig. 6
C–G;
Fig. S8
).
Collectively, these data demonstrated that H
2
S-mediated S-persulfidation of HNF1α at Cys241 suppressed hepatic PCSK9 expression and conferred protection against HCD-induced atherosclerosis in
Apoe
−/−
mice. This provided
in vivo
evidence linking HNF1α S-persulfidation to lipid metabolism and vascular pathology, highlighting a novel regulatory axis with potential therapeutic relevance.
4
Discussion
In this study, we present a novel integrative strategy to uncover functional S-persulfidation targets, addressing the limitations of conventional proteomic workflows that often overlook low-abundance proteins such as TFs. By merging published S-persulfidation datasets across
Homo sapiens
,
Mus musculus
, and
Arabidopsis thaliana
with the Oximouse redox proteomic database, we leveraged the concept that S-persulfidation may serve as a protective mechanism against irreversible cysteine overoxidation. This cross-omics screening strategy identified HNF1α Cys241 as a previously uncharacterized S-persulfidation site, and its functional significance was confirmed through structural, biochemical, and physiological analyses.
Our study identifies Cys241 of HNF1α as a specific target of H
2
S-induced S-persulfidation. LC-MS/MS with a broad search strategy detected persulfidation (–SSH) exclusively at Cys241 in NaHS-treated samples, while other cysteine modifications such as sulfenylation (–SOH) and sulfonylation (–SO
3
H) were absent or not specific. The C241S mutant completely abolished this modification, and the comparable persulfidation levels observed in WT, C241S, and C241S + NaHS groups further confirmed site specificity. MD simulations and structural remodeling revealed that persulfidation at Cys241 induces conformational changes by pulling helix H via an extensive hydrogen bond network, bringing loop1 closer to the POUs domain and thereby weakening the interactions of both POUs and POU
H
domains with DNA. Although the addition of a single sulfur atom is chemically conservative, complementary structural, SPR, and DNA-binding assays indicate that this modification directly perturbs the DNA-binding domain, providing a mechanistic basis for functional inhibition. Moreover, in an HCD-induced oxidative stress model, exogenous H
2
S restored Cys241 persulfidation and alleviated PCSK9 upregulation, underscoring a protective role of this modification in preserving HNF1α activity under pro-oxidative conditions.
Notably, recent advances have highlighted cysteinyl-tRNA synthetase (CARS) as a co-translational generator of protein persulfidation and polysulfidation, representing a conceptual breakthrough in understanding how sulfur-based redox signals can be precisely installed on selected cysteine residues [
[76]
,
[77]
,
[78]
,
[79]
,
[80]
]. This elegant model might provide a plausible biochemical explanation for the basal persulfidation of HNF1α detected in our study (
Fig. 3
F), which can be further modulated by exogenous H
2
S donors. These observations support a regulatory framework in which Cys241 functions as a reversible, redox-sensitive cysteine switch, enabling HNF1α to respond dynamically to the thiol redox state. Our findings therefore complement this emerging paradigm and extend its functional implications to transcriptional control of lipid metabolism.
Transcriptomic profiling of CSE knockout mice identified PCSK9 as a downstream target suppressed by S-persulfidated HNF1α. Given that PCSK9 facilitates LDLR degradation and elevates circulating LDL-C levels, its downregulation through HNF1α persulfidation highlights a redox-sensitive mechanism contributing to lipid homeostasis. Consistently, in an HCD-induced atherosclerosis model, HNF1α persulfidation mitigated lipid accumulation and vascular lesions. Notably, loss of CSE-derived H
2
S in knockout mice decreased HNF1α persulfidation and enhanced PCSK9 expression, thereby promoting susceptibility to plaque formation upon HNF1α-WT AAV transduction. These results demonstrate that endogenous H
2
S functions in a manner similar to exogenous donors by maintaining HNF1α persulfidation and restraining PCSK9 transcription, reinforcing the physiological relevance of this regulatory axis.
Our transcriptomic profiling further provides insights into the relationship between H
2
S signaling and hepatic lipid secretion. Human hepatocytes predominantly export lipids in the form of very low-density lipoproteins (VLDL). However, in CSE-deficient mouse livers, the expression of genes involved in VLDL assembly and secretion—including ApoB, ApoE, Mttp, Arf 1, COP1, Dgat1, Dgat2, Ces3a, Ces3b, and Sar1b—showed no significant alterations compared with wild-type controls (
Table S10
). These findings suggest that H
2
S deficiency may not substantially perturb the hepatic lipid export machinery, indicating that the metabolic effects observed in our study are more likely mediated through transcriptional regulation rather than through gross changes in lipid secretion phenotypes.
In addition to its DNA-binding function, HNF1α also interacts with transcriptional coactivators such as p300/CBP to regulate target gene expression [
81
,
82
]. Recruitment of p300 to the PCSK9 promoter has been shown to enhance its transcription [
83
]. While our current work primarily focused on the DNA-binding regulation of HNF1α, it will be of interest to investigate whether Cys241 persulfidation also modulates HNF1α–p300/CBP interactions, potentially representing an additional redox-sensitive layer of transcriptional control.
Our findings further highlight the functional importance of Cys241 persulfidation in regulating cholesterol metabolism. Although the C241S mutation abolishes this modification, we did not observe a basal phenotype on cholesterol levels in C241S HNF1α-expressing mice. This can be plausibly explained by the limited availability of endogenous H
2
S under HCD conditions. As shown in previous studies, the plasma H
2
S level was decreased in
Apoe
−/−
mice fed with high-fat diet compared with that in WT mice [
84
,
85
]. Also, our measurements revealed that HCD significantly lowered plasma H
2
S level and reduced H
2
S content and production rate in hepatic tissues of rats (
Fig. S9
). Based on these abovementioned data, we reason that the endogenous pool of H
2
S is insufficient to fully persulfidate HNF1α at Cys241 under these conditions. Consequently, both WT and C241S mice are expected to display comparable cholesterol levels in the absence of exogenous H
2
S supplementation. This interpretation, while consistent with existing H
2
S measurements, underscores the conditional and context-dependent nature of HNF1α persulfidation in metabolic regulation.
From a translational perspective, this study provides new therapeutic insights into lipometabolic disturbance-related diseases. PCSK9 monoclonal antibodies, which are already clinically approved, work by preventing PCSK9 from binding to LDLR, thereby blocking LDLR degradation and effectively lowering circulating LDL-C levels [
26
,
86
]. However, their widespread use is limited by high costs and notable adverse effects [
[86]
,
[87]
,
[88]
]. Therefore, new approaches to intervene in the PCSK9 pathway within the cell would open a new avenue to develop next-generation PCSK9 inhibitor. Based on our findings, S-persulfidation of HNF1α offers a novel intracellular mechanism to suppress PCSK9 transcription. The convergence of HNF1α modulation and PCSK9 repression thus points to a promising strategy for combination therapies in lipid disorders induced cardiac-cerebral vascular diseases.
Beyond metabolic pathways, our analyses also considered gene ontology categories related to cellular components and molecular functions. These complementary perspectives may help reveal aspects such as the subcellular availability of H
2
S, the evolutionary conservation of persulfidated targets, and potential technical bias across proteomic studies. While not the central focus of this work, these analyses provide an additional layer of insight into the global characteristics of persulfidation and are presented in the Supplementary Materials (
Table S2
).
In addition, analysis of the Oximouse dataset revealed a distinct subset of proteins whose oxidation levels decreased with age (
Fig. 2
A). This finding is intriguing, as the conventional paradigm often emphasizes age-associated increases in oxidative stress and protein oxidation [
89
]. Instead, it suggests that aging may involve selective redox remodeling, rather than being solely a process of cumulative oxidative damage. Such redox remodeling appears to be a selective and adaptive response, potentially reflecting the activation of thiol-reducing systems—such as the thioredoxin and glutaredoxin pathways—that maintain the redox status of key proteins [
90
,
91
]. Alternatively, these proteins may undergo compensatory shifts in various PTMs, to protect cysteines and modulate protein function. These findings raise several important questions: Does the observed reduction in oxidation contribute to the preservation or even enhancement of protein function during aging? And to what extent do alternative cysteine PTMs mediate this effect? Future studies aimed at answering these questions will be essential to refine our understanding of the complex and dynamic redox landscape of aging, and to illuminate the functional interplay among distinct redox-based PTMs.
Looking forward, advancements in data-independent acquisition proteomics, chemical enrichment strategies, and single-cell proteomics are expected to increase the depth and coverage of S-persulfidation profiling [
92
,
93
]. These technologies will likely uncover a more comprehensive landscape of redox-sensitive modifications, including those on traditionally “invisible” low-abundance proteins. Moreover, coupling these datasets with machine learning-guided structural modeling may enable prediction of functional consequences of cysteine modifications [
94
,
95
], accelerating the identification of novel regulatory mechanisms in aging, metabolism, and disease.
In summary, this study highlights a critical blind spot in current S-persulfidation proteomics—the underrepresentation of low-abundance regulatory proteins such as TFs. By integrating multi-omics data mining with comprehensive biological validation, including LC-MS/MS analysis, structural biology, molecular and cellular biology, transcriptomics, and
in vivo
mouse models, we systematically investigated the biological function of S-persulfidated HNF1α in metabolic and cardiovascular diseases. Our findings not only broaden the spectrum of proteins potentially regulated by S-persulfidation but also provide a conceptual and methodological framework for future studies aimed at elucidating the roles of S-persulfidation in diverse biological processes.
